etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English institucioun, from Old French institution, from Latin institūtiō, from instituō (“to set up”), from in- (“in, on”) + statuō (“to set up, establish”).

definitions.definition: A custom or practice of a society or community.
A  long established and respected organization, particularly one involved with education, public service, or charity work.
The building or buildings which house such an organization.
(informal) Any long established and respected place or business.

quote.citation: 2009 February 19, Gareth Lewis, “Giles Coren slams Winchester pub The Wykeham Arms”, in Southern Daily Echo‎[1]:
quote.text: [quoting Giles Coren] "The Wykeham Arms [a pub] is destroyed. They have turned a great old English institution into a shameful clip-joint. It's a shuddering, howling tragedy."

definitions.definition: (informal) A person long established in a place, position, or field.

quote.citation: 1894, James George Frazer, The Golden Bough‎[2]:
quote.text: Accordingly if we can show that a barbarous custom, like that of the priesthood of Nemi, has existed elsewhere; if we can detect the motives which led to its institution; if we can prove that these motives have operated widely, perhaps universally, in human society...

definitions.definition: (Christianity) The act by which a bishop commits a cure of souls to a priest. (Can we clean up(+) this sense?)
(obsolete) That which institutes or instructs, particularly a textbook or system of elements or rules.
